issues.legal_issue: Removing a landlord’s ability to seek eviction for bona fide personal use from non-residential premises, while retaining that ground for residential premises, violates the constitutional guarantee of equality when the distinction has no rational connection to the rent-control law’s purpose.
material_facts: The rent-control law originally allowed a landlord to seek eviction for bona fide personal use from both residential and non-residential premises.
An amendment removed that ground of eviction for non-residential premises while retaining it for residential premises.
The law’s stated purposes included controlling rents and protecting tenants against mala fide attempts by landlords to obtain eviction.
The amendment’s stated reasons included hardship to tenants of non-residential premises and misuse of the personal-use ground by some landlords.
The landlord asserted that, after retiring from government service, he bona fide required the rented shop for his own use.
issues.conclusion: The provisions removing the personal-use eviction ground for non-residential premises were declared constitutionally invalid and struck down. The original provisions were restored, so a landlord may seek eviction from non-residential premises on the ground that the landlord requires them for personal use.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14 of the Constitution, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia distinguishing those grouped together from those left out, and that differentia must have a rational relation to the statute’s object. The Court relied on Budhan Choudhary v. State of Bihar, Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar, U.P. Electric Power and Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P., and Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar for the classification test. It also relied on Rattan Arya v. State of Tamil Nadu, which invalidated an unrelated distinction between residential and non-residential tenants, and Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar, which observed that a landlord’s bona fide need stands on the same footing for residential and commercial premises.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_rent_control_rule and commercial_personal_need_eviction_removed and residential_personal_need_eviction_retained and rent_protections_apply_to_both_building_types and law_aims_to_protect_tenants_from_mala_fide_eviction and building_use_type_does_not_distinguish_bona_fide_owner_need

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_control: A party challenges the constitutionality of a rule governing eviction of tenants from rented premises.
predicates.commercial_personal_need_eviction_remove: The legislature removes a landlord’s ability to seek eviction of a tenant from premises used for business on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide personal need.
predicates.residential_personal_need_eviction_retai: The law continues to allow a landlord to seek eviction from residential premises on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide personal need.
predicates.rent_protections_apply_to_both_building_: The law’s other rent and tenancy protections apply to both residential and business premises.
predicates.law_aims_to_protect_tenants_from_mala_fi: The law is intended, among other things, to protect tenants from landlords’ mala fide attempts to obtain eviction.
predicates.building_use_type_does_not_distinguish_b: The use of a building as residential or business premises does not make a landlord’s bona fide need for personal use materially different.

issues.definition: When a rent-control rule challenged constitutionally removes personal-need eviction for business premises but retains it for residential premises, despite applying the same tenant protections to both and without a relevant difference in bona fide owner need, the amendment is invalid.
